video_title: Nate Silver On What the Polls Say — And What His Gut’s Telling Him | The Ezra Klein Show
gist: A week before the 2026 midterms, Nate Silver tells Ezra Klein his model gives Democrats a 70%+ Senate chance and 90%+ House chance (about 22 seats on average), driven by an ~11-point anti-GOP swing tied to Iran-war gas prices, Trump's record-low approval and strong Democratic recruits. He flags correlated polling error risk concentrated in heartland states like Kansas and Iowa, and an emerging AI/data-center backlash as a sleeper issue for 2026 and 2028.

insights.claim: Nate Silver's model gives Democrats a 70%+ chance of winning the Senate roughly two weeks before the 2026 midterms, despite needing to flip at least four Republican-held seats including states Trump won by double digits.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: A Democratic Senate flip has moved from long-shot to base case, raising odds of divided government gridlock for Trump's final two years.
insights.quote: Democrats are at a 70 plus percent chance of winning the Senate in your model

insights.claim: The average midterm shifts the environment about 7.5 points against the president's party versus the prior presidential year; in 2026 the shift looks closer to 11 points.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: An 11-point uniform swing turns Trump+10-13 states like Ohio into toss-ups.
insights.quote: in the average midterm the environment shifts by 7 and 1/2 points against the president's party versus the previous presidential year. Um this year it looks more like 11 points.

insights.claim: Silver's Texas Senate math: a Trump+13 state minus an 11-point Democratic environment shift yields R+2, and Ken Paxton's weakness as a candidate (candidate effects worth up to ~5 points) could plausibly flip it to D+2 for James Talarico.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Candidate quality is the marginal swing factor once the national environment does most of the work.

insights.claim: Midterm backlash against the president's party is one of the most durable regularities in American elections, with only 1998 and 2002 as clear exceptions, undermining the post-2024 idea of a permanent conservative 'vibe shift'.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Structural midterm reversion should be the default assumption, not narratives of permanent realignment.

insights.claim: If Democrats lose one of Maine or Michigan they still have a Senate path, but losing both would probably end any Democratic Senate flip.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Maine and Michigan are the key swing seats to watch on election night.
insights.quote: Michigan and Maine, if Democrats were to lose one of them, they'd still have a chance. If they were to lose both, then probably game over for a Democratic Senate flip.

insights.claim: Silver is wary of the Maine race because Susan Collins beat her polls by about nine points in her last election and Maine has had little polling, even though Democrat Troy Jackson leads.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Persistent candidate-specific polling error makes Maine the most likely Democratic disappointment.

insights.claim: A plausible bad Democratic night involves losing all the toss-ups by about a point each (Talarico, Jackson, Turek losing; El-Sayed squeaking out a recount win), which sits in the thick part of the probability distribution.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Investors should not treat a 70% Senate probability as certainty; correlated toss-up losses are very feasible.

insights.claim: Silver's model gives Democrats a 90%+ chance of winning the House but that translates to only about 22 seats gained on average, far below waves like 63 seats in 2010 or roughly 41 in 2018, because redistricting and voter self-sorting have shrunk swing districts.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: A Democratic House is near-certain but the majority size will likely be modest absent a polling miss.

insights.claim: Republicans gained about three House seats from redistricting by eliminating majority-minority districts in states like Louisiana, Alabama and Tennessee, while Texas and Florida Republican maps became riskier in a wave environment.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Aggressive gerrymanders can backfire in wave years, making House outcomes asymmetric to Democratic upside.

insights.claim: Republican House outcomes range from holding Democrats to about 10 House seats and keeping the Senate to a complete 1994-style disaster, with the outcome hinging on Republican turnout since Democratic turnout will be high and persuasion is done.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: GOP turnout is the key unknown determining the magnitude of the result.
insights.quote: the persuasion part of this is done. I'd be shocked if Democratic turnout wasn't high by midterm standards.

insights.claim: Silver's rule of thumb: always ask what happens if polls are off by three or four points in the same direction across every Senate race, since errors are correlated.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Treat race-level probabilities as correlated bets, not independent ones.
insights.quote: Always ask yourself, what if they're off by three or four points in the same direction in every race.

insights.claim: Polling error has not consistently favored Republicans in Trump-era midterms: 2018 was one of the most accurate polling years ever and 2022 was similar, while in 2025's New Jersey and Virginia races polls underestimated Democrats by five to ten points.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: The Trump-overperformance prior applies mainly to presidential years when Trump is on the ballot.
insights.quote: In New Jersey, Virginia last year, the polls were five to 10 points low on on Democrats

insights.claim: Polls missing low on Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024 was the death knell for the 'gold standard' polling approach of surveying people and weighting only to census demographics.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Polls are now models with judgment-laden adjustments, increasing pollster herding and methodological dispersion.
insights.quote: the three presidential years was kind of the death knell for the gold standard of polling

insights.claim: Ann Selzer's final 2024 Iowa poll showed Kamala Harris up about three while other polls showed roughly Trump+9, and it ended up off by about 13-15 points.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Even top-rated pollsters who refuse to adjust raw data can miss badly in the current response environment.

insights.claim: A modern poll is effectively a mini model with polling-flavored inputs, and pollsters iterate adjustments like a restaurant tuning spice levels in response to complaints, since they face large reputational stakes on final-week accuracy.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Poll outputs embed pollster assumptions, so cross-poll agreement may reflect shared corrections rather than independent signal.
insights.quote: a poll is kind of almost like a mini model with polling flavored inputs

insights.claim: In wave or unexpected elections pollsters sometimes lowball the magnitude, e.g. 1994 turned a bad Clinton year into a terrible one, and 2014 differential turnout produced a nine-seat Democratic Senate loss.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Error risk is skewed toward a larger-than-polled wave when enthusiasm gaps are large.

insights.claim: Likely-voter screens based on self-reported enthusiasm produce very Democratic samples, while screens based on other data such as vote history produce more modest Democratic results.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Spread between pollsters partly reflects the likely-voter methodology choice.

insights.claim: Early voting data shows low-propensity voters (those who voted in at most one of the past three elections) are quite Democratic so far; if Democratic low-propensity voters turn out and GOP ones don't, polls could underestimate Democrats.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: A possible source of Democratic upside surprise relative to polls.

insights.claim: Silver's model includes fat tails allowing polls to be off by five to seven points, but a scenario where Democrats only flip North Carolina in the Senate and the House is close would defy what is known about midterms.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: A large Republican overperformance is a tail risk, not a central scenario.

insights.claim: Silver's gut versus model in 2026: unlike 2024, when he could list about 21 reasons the environment favored Trump and only four or five for Harris, fundamentals now overwhelmingly favor Democrats, yet he worries more about state polls (e.g. Kansas, Iowa) being wrong than the national environment.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: National House environment is the safer call; heartland Senate races carry the most polling-miss risk.
insights.quote: I worry more about the state polls being wrong than the national race being being miscalibrated.

themes.theme: Regional patterns, candidate quality and the Democratic coalition

insights.claim: Democrats are overperforming more in redder heartland states (Texas, Kansas, Iowa) than in bluer states like Michigan and Minnesota, which also makes Democrats nervous because heartland states are where polls have recently overstated them.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Red-state Democratic leads carry the highest polling-error risk.

insights.claim: High gas and diesel prices hit colder Midwestern states hardest because diesel is consumed by agriculture, trucking, petroleum and home heating oil, helping explain Democratic gains in heartland battlegrounds.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Energy price shocks have region-specific political effects concentrated in agricultural and trucking states.

insights.claim: A 'last in, first out' dynamic may be at work: groups that most recently joined the Trump coalition, such as Hispanics, working-class whites and young men, are moving back toward Democrats or not voting.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Trump-era coalition gains are fragile without Trump on the ballot.
insights.quote: the one group you do not want to rely on to turn out in a midterm is usually young men.

insights.claim: Ezra Klein's 'moderation wins' thesis: in red states Democrats deliberately nominated moderate, independent-seeming candidates, while in bluer states like Maine, Michigan and Minnesota they took more risk with left candidates and are underperforming relative to the environment.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Candidate ideology may cost Democrats several points in purple states.

insights.claim: In Michigan, Jocelyn Benson leads the governor's race by about eight points while Abdul El-Sayed leads the Senate race by about three to three and a half, implying a four to four-and-a-half point candidate-quality gap that Silver attributes partly to moderation.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Quantifies the cost of a progressive nominee in a purple state.

insights.claim: Democrats in states with Democratic trifectas and critiques of liberal governance, such as Minnesota (Peggy Flanagan up only 3.5-4), Oregon (Tina Kotek up only 1-2) and New York (Kathy Hochul by a tepid margin), are underperforming amid an anti-incumbent mood about who has power over voters' lives.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Local governance dissatisfaction can offset a favorable national environment.

insights.claim: Tim Walz's approval rating is about 17 points underwater, to the point that he abandoned plans to run for another term, making Minnesota ground zero for backlash against Democratic governance.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Shows state-level incumbent weakness even in a Democratic year.

insights.claim: Ezra Klein observes almost no connection between which Democratic candidates are omnipresent on social media and podcasts (El-Sayed, Talarico, Ossoff clips) and which are actually overperforming in polls (often low-profile ones like Sherrod Brown, Mary Peltola, Roy Cooper).
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Online attention is a poor proxy for electoral strength.

insights.claim: Florida has become redder than Texas, which Silver attributes roughly 75% to politically self-selected migration and 25% to a self-reinforcing Democratic Party death spiral; Florida registration keeps getting redder even as Democrats regain registration edges in the Midwest and Pennsylvania.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Florida is structurally lost for Democrats even in a wave year.
insights.quote: I think it's 75% migration and 25% kind of a death spiral for the Democratic Party that might be self-reinforcing.

insights.claim: Money is generally overrated in high-profile races like Senate and governor due to diminishing returns, though it matters more for House frontier races and state legislatures; the Republican financial advantage likely translates to roughly 50/50 ad impressions because candidate-raised money buys cheaper ad rates.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Headline fundraising gaps, including Musk's spending, overstate actual persuasion impact.
insights.quote: I think money is generally overrated in politics

insights.claim: Elon Musk is personally financing a large share of the Republican midterm campaign, around $400 million or more.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Concentrated tech-donor money ties GOP to tech-right interests, including on AI policy.

insights.claim: Klein argues Democrats are entering an era of elder millennial talent (El-Sayed, AOC, Rob Sand, Talarico, Ossoff, Buttigieg) more native to the current communication era, with Silver likening it to a 'Steph Curry effect' from Obama.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Signals a generational turnover in Democratic leadership heading into 2028.

insights.claim: Post-election narratives about progressives vs. moderates will hinge on whether races are called on election night rather than on margins; an El-Sayed loss would be a very bad narrative for progressives regardless of the Senate outcome.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Michigan's result will shape Democratic factional strategy into 2028.

themes.theme: Trump's weakening position and GOP dynamics

insights.claim: Silver argues that if the midterms go as polls suggest, they would mark the end of the Trump era, leaving Trump a 'super lame duck' akin to Bush after 2006 as the 2028 campaign begins immediately.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Expect reduced legislative leverage and policy volatility from a lame-duck White House.
insights.quote: If the election goes roughly as the polls say it will go, then in some ways it would mark the end of the Trump era.

insights.claim: Trump's approval rating is now lower than after January 6th, as low as it has ever been.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Historically low approval underpins the wave environment.

insights.claim: Trump's approval decline is statistically correlated with gas prices plus a time trend, with a large drop around the April 2025 'Liberation Day' tariffs.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Energy prices are a key driver of presidential approval and thus political risk.
insights.quote: If you want to like model it statistically, then you know, it's quite correlated with gas prices, frankly.

insights.claim: Silver believes Democrats would not be favored for the Senate if Trump had not gone to war with Iran and pushed gas prices into the mid-$4 per gallon range.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: The Iran war's oil price shock is the proximate cause of the GOP's midterm collapse.

insights.claim: Trump's first-term strong economy acted as a halo that made Democratic culture-war critiques seem marginal; with economic satisfaction gone, culture-war messaging now seems desperate, compounded by fatigue and Trump being 80.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Economic perceptions gate the effectiveness of culture-war politics.

insights.claim: Trump could have ended the Texas Senate primary and made John Cornyn the nominee, which would have strengthened Republicans; his midterm strategy, including a $5,000 check promise, centers on himself rather than party success.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Trump's personal incentives diverge from the GOP's institutional interest in holding Congress.

insights.claim: Republicans have done badly in elections where Trump is dominant but not on the ballot (2018, specials, runoffs, Supreme Court races, ballot initiatives) because his low-propensity voters, who also don't answer polls, will not turn out for candidates like Roger Marshall or Ken Paxton.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Polling bias toward Democrats is less likely in midterms since Trump's hidden voters stay home.
insights.quote: the one magic trick that Trump has is to get a certain type of usually disengaged voter to kind of like crawl on glass to vote for him when he himself is on on the ballot.

insights.claim: Silver says that if Republicans lose the Senate, Pete Hegseth should be among the first blamed for the Iran war with an ambiguous plan; Klein expects Hegseth to be fired after the midterms but replaced by another loyalist.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Personnel changes after the midterms are unlikely to restore checks on Trump's decision-making.

themes.theme: AI, data centers and market risk

insights.claim: Silver thinks AI may be a bigger issue in the 2026 midterms than people assume and could be, alongside the economy, the biggest issue of 2028.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: AI policy is becoming an electoral liability and a 2028 campaign axis.

insights.claim: Economist data shows the closer Trump voters live to data centers, the more likely they are to flip to Democrats, which may be a hidden factor in Midwest Democratic gains.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Data center buildout carries local political backlash risk that could constrain siting and permitting.

insights.claim: Data centers are roughly an 80/20 issue against them, and when asked whether AI should accelerate or slow down, about 3% say accelerate versus about 60% slow down.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Strong public opposition to AI acceleration creates regulatory and political risk for AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: data centers are like a 80/20 issue against data centers now, roughly.

insights.claim: Klein argues Trump backs data centers despite their unpopularity because he believes in an AI race with China and because the AI-driven stock market is his only good economic indicator; an AI sentiment shift would collapse it, leaving high rates, debt and anemic growth.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Administration AI policy is tied to protecting AI-driven equity valuations.
insights.quote: if the AI boom, if something shift sentiment then the one economic indicator Trump has that is looking good for him, which is the stock market,

insights.claim: Investor anxiety about an AI bubble is growing and becoming more sophisticated, framed as whether the economy can land the plane on a narrow runway without tested instrumentation.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: AI bubble risk is a live market concern heading into year-end.
insights.quote: I think the AI bubble argument's getting more sophisticated

insights.claim: Silver says the most obvious late-cycle surprise would be a market downturn, especially with oil prices rising sharply again in the Middle East in the past week or two, which would further hurt Trump.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Oil and equity volatility are the key tail risks into the election.

insights.claim: Post-election analysts may look for an AI backlash by checking whether Republicans underperformed by around three points in states with data center construction.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: Evidence of data-center backlash would raise political risk for hyperscaler buildouts.

insights.claim: Klein sees elevated tail risk in Trump's final two years, including a recession or correlated financial crisis, escalation involving Iran, Israel or Russia-Ukraine, and AI incidents, with a weakened, aging president surrounded by loyalists poorly positioned to respond.
insights.speaker: Ezra Klein
insights.so_what: Investors should price higher macro and geopolitical tail risk through 2028.
insights.quote: the world feels full of risk to me.

insights.claim: Silver recommends Robert Gordon's The Rise and Fall of American Growth, noting that the Industrial Revolution produced terrible living conditions for many years before broad gains, a caution against the AI-optimist analogy.
insights.speaker: Nate Silver
insights.so_what: AI's welfare gains may lag disruption by years.
